summary: Specifies a network proxy that uses Multicast DNS to automatically fill the wide-area unicast DNS namespace with records describing devices and services found on the local link. This lets service discovery work beyond a single network segment.

eli5.summary: Your home printer announces itself only to the people in the room. This helper relays that announcement so people elsewhere can find it too.

subtitle: A proxy that answers ordinary DNS queries by asking Multicast DNS on the local link, so service discovery works across networks.

tldr.problem: Multicast DNS packets stay on one link, so devices like printers cannot be found from other links, and filling the unicast DNS by hand or by device updates is laborious.
tldr.mechanism: A Discovery Proxy is made authoritative for a subdomain per link. When a unicast query arrives, it queries the link with Multicast DNS, translates names from .local to the delegated domain, and replies.
tldr.outcome: Remote clients can use DNS-based Service Discovery over unicast with no changes to existing devices, and the proxy sends no packets when idle.

today: RFC 8766 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It relies on RFC 8765 (DNS Push Notifications), which it expects to be the long-term notification mechanism.

sections.title: The Problem and the Idea
sections.content:
Multicast DNS (mDNS) and DNS-based Service Discovery (DNS-SD) work well on a single link. On a larger network joined by IP routing, link-local mDNS packets are by design not passed on to other links. Flooding multicast across links would add expensive traffic, especially on Wi-Fi, where multicast is sent at lower data rates and is not acknowledged.

Other ways to fill the unicast DNS have drawbacks. Manual zone configuration is labor intensive and error prone. Having devices send DNS Update requires update keys, which proved onerous for simple devices like printers and network cameras. So the RFC specifies a Discovery Proxy: a hybrid that uses mDNS to find records on its link on demand and makes matching records visible in unicast DNS.

A descriptive DNS name is chosen for each link, and an NS record delegates it to a Discovery Proxy on that link. The proxy uses a pull model: until a remote client asks, it sends nothing. A push model, where a proxy updates a remote DNS server, would fail because mDNS devices stay silent until queried, so the proxy could not learn which names exist.
sections.eli5: Instead of shouting about every printer all day, the helper only looks around when someone asks. That keeps the network quiet.

sections.title: A Proxy, Not a Multicast Relay
sections.content:
A Discovery Proxy does not forward multicast packets, so there is no risk of forwarding loops or traffic storms. It acts as a proxy for remote clients, performing queries on their behalf and reporting results back. The RFC compares it to phoning a colleague at work and asking them to read out the printers they see, or logging in over ssh and running a browse command.

It can be seen as a custom remote procedure call protocol for the mDNS APIs on the proxy device. The same mDNS caching rules apply as for any local client. The RFC defines 'on the same link' as hosts where the link-layer payload arrives unmodified, so repeaters, bridges and switches are fine but an IP router that changes the IP header is not.
sections.eli5: The helper does not pass your shout along. It just goes and looks, then tells you what it found.

sections.title: Delegated Subdomains and Name Translation
sections.content:
A proxy is typically authoritative for four or more subdomains delegated to it with NS records: one for service discovery records (which may contain rich text such as spaces), one for host names, and subdomains for IPv4 and IPv6 reverse mapping under in-addr.arpa and ip6.arpa. Host names SHOULD be limited to letters, digits and hyphens. A proxy MAY use a single rich-text domain for everything, but MUST NOT support only the letter-digit-hyphen domain.

For a query such as _ipp._tcp.Building 1.example.com. PTR, the proxy asks mDNS for _ipp._tcp.local., then rewrites .local in owner names and in record data to the delegated domain. SRV target host names go to the letter-digit-hyphen domain when one is configured. Reverse queries are issued unchanged as mDNS queries and the .local answer is rewritten.

Other rules: names are passed as-is in UTF-8, with no Punycode or other text-encoding translation. Link-local and, in some cases, private addresses and records that point to them SHOULD be suppressed for off-link clients. For NSEC queries the proxy issues an ANY query and builds a record covering only the one name asked about.
sections.eli5: On the local street everyone is 'something dot local'. The helper swaps that ending for the real address of the building before telling you, so your answer makes sense far away.

sections.title: Timing, Caching and Answer Aggregation
sections.content:
A proxy cannot know when it has heard every mDNS answer, so waiting is a trade-off. The RFC defines five cases. For a standard DNS query with nothing cached, the proxy issues mDNS queries, replies as soon as any answer arrives, and after six seconds with no answer returns a negative response (no error, no answer, never NXDOMAIN). With an answer cached, it replies at once and sends no mDNS query. For standard queries, TTLs MUST be capped at ten seconds.

Long-Lived Queries (LLQ) and DNS Push Notifications solve the waiting problem: the proxy answers from cache immediately, keeps querying the link, and sends update messages as new answers appear, with TTLs returned unmodified. Clients supporting unicast DNS-SD SHOULD implement DNS Push Notifications, and the RFC expects that only Push Notifications will continue to be supported in the long run.
sections.eli5: If the helper already knows the answer, it says so right away. If not, it looks around for a few seconds, and if you ask it to keep watching, it calls back when something new shows up.

sections.title: Administrative Records and DNSSEC
sections.content:
Some records in a delegated zone describe the zone itself and have no .local counterpart, so the proxy MUST answer them immediately. In the SOA record the SERIAL field MUST be zero, MINIMUM SHOULD be 10, and the recommended REFRESH, RETRY and EXPIRE are 7200, 3600 and 86400. Where several proxies serve a link, the parent zone MUST list NS records for all of them, and NS targets MUST NOT fall inside a zone delegated to a proxy.

Queries for SOA, NS or DS below the zone apex get an immediate negative answer. Proxies MUST answer SRV queries such as _dns-push-tls._tcp.<zone> positively only if they implement that feature, and MUST return an immediate negative answer for DNS Update SRV queries. With DNSSEC the proxy needs the signing keys because only online signing applies.
sections.eli5: A few questions are about the helper itself, not about the room. The helper answers those instantly instead of going to look.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A service proves its presence only by answering link-local multicast on the link. If stronger security is wanted, the RFC says not to use the Discovery Proxy and to use authenticated secure DNS Update instead.

Privacy is a concern: services appearing and disappearing in a domain like My House.example.com could show when a mobile device is at home, and exposing reverse zones to the public can leak host names. Firewalls, split-view DNS and VPNs can protect this. For denial of service, a proxy MUST rate-limit mDNS queries to suit the link; for 802.11b/g/n/ac Wi-Fi it RECOMMENDS 20 mDNS query packets per second.
sections.eli5: Anyone who can ask the helper can learn what is in the room, so keep the helper behind a locked door, and do not let one person ask so fast that the room gets noisy.

sections.title: Compatibility and Deployment Notes
sections.content:
No changes to existing devices are required. Existing mDNS devices work with a proxy, and existing clients that support DNS-SD over unicast DNS also work. The RFC says this client support began in Mac OS X 10.4 Tiger in April 2005 and also appears in Windows 10. It notes that unicast discovery has been used for several years at IETF meetings to make terminal room printers discoverable.

On IPv6, each link may have two unrelated .local. zones, one for IPv4 and one for IPv6. For now a proxy is RECOMMENDED to use a single domain name for both and to query using both IPv4 and IPv6, combining the results. The RFC has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: Your old gadgets do not need to change anything. The helper works with what is already there.
